title: Medicine Against Itself: Toward a Nonlinear Neuropsychopharmacology
content: Contemporary clinical medicine reasons with an epistemic apparatus inherited, largely unrevised, from a nineteenth-century picture of nature: the linear and deterministic mechanism whose canonical statement runs from Newton’s laws of motion to Laplace’s calculating intelligence, for which a complete specification of the present fixes the entire future of a system. The living bodies that medicine proposes to treat have never behaved this way. This essay does not question the randomized controlled trial as a method. It questions the trial’s promotion to sovereign, the quiet assumption that the averaged answer it returns is the answer to the question actually asked at the bedside. Once a drug leaves the mean patient of the phase-III curve and reaches the single patient in the room, the metaphysics the trial tacitly carries comes apart: diagnostic categories reveal themselves as soft thresholds laid over continuous distributions, mechanisms of action prove dose-reversing and history-dependent, and the system under intervention, governed by strictly nonlinear dynamics, carries the memory of every molecule it has ever met. A mature molecular neuropsychopharmacology, the essay argues, rests on three commitments taken together: an epistemological move from averaged inference to nonlinear trajectory; a pharmacological move from equilibrium binding constants to hysteretic, path-dependent receptor dynamics; and an ontological move from the Cartesian pilot to the embodied subject described by Merleau-Ponty. Read together, these commitments recast the psychotropic act as a change in the topology of a patient’s lived world, and recast the clinician as an architect of homeostasis rather than a herald of protocols.
